carryoverIn.title: Second Pick Wins
carryoverIn.pitch: A visitor picks a three-flip coin pattern, a smug bot picks its own after seeing it, and a flip-by-flip race decides whose pattern shows up first. Every first pick loses at least two thirds of the time to the best reply, so the visitor runs ten million simulated races and watches the bot's edge settle on exact fractions such as 2 to 1. Then the visitor takes the second pick and the table flips; a red-and-black card mode with tricks shows the same effect in a real deck.
carryoverIn.whyNow: Timeless. The game is fair in each pick yet decided by the order of choosing, which makes it a durable argument-loser.

research.summary: In Penney's game two players each pick a short heads-tails pattern and the one that appears first in a fair coin sequence wins. Because picking is sequential, the second picker can answer any three-flip pattern with a reply that is strictly more likely to appear first (at least 2 to 1 for length 3, computed here from the leading-number formula). A short rule builds the reply, and Conway's leading-number method gives exact odds. A red/black card version with tricks (Humble-Nishiyama) exists. The page can show the payoff matrix for lengths 3 to 5, exact odds next to a seeded Monte Carlo, and expected waiting times. At length 3 the winning reply never has a longer average wait than the pattern it beats, but at length 4 it can (THTH, wait 20, beats HTHH, wait 18, with probability 9/14), which is where the loss feels unfair.

facts.claim: In Penney's game the second chooser can answer any three-flip pattern with a pattern strictly more likely to appear first; HTH answered by HHT wins 2 to 1 (two thirds).
Conway's leading-number method gives the odds between two patterns: odds for B over A are (AA-AB):(BB-BA); a no-arbitrage derivation was published in 2019 and in Theory and Decision in 2026.

Longer average wait does not decide the winner: THTH (average wait 20 flips) beats HTHH (average wait 18) with probability 9/14.

ideas.title: Moon Ferry
ideas.pitch: A visitor skippers a slow ferry across an invented strait where the tidal stream outruns the engine. They scrub an hour-by-hour stream atlas, read the day's tide table, pick a departure time and drag waypoints, and the boat then sails the plan while the arrows swing round and a shoal ledge dries and floods. Afterwards a solver reveals the fastest possible passage as a ghost boat and paints arrival-time isochrones that lean with the stream, so the visitor sees which minutes the moon took.
ideas.whyNow: October is king-tide season: station tables list a new-moon spring-tide window on Oct 10-11, 2026 and a larger perigean peak around Oct 26-28, so the autumn's strongest streams are due. The daily passage reads the real moon age, and the idea stays good all year because every coast keeps a tide table.

research.summary: Tidal navigation is a map that changes with the clock. Stream atlases print one chartlet per hour relative to high water at a standard port, with arrows whose paired numbers give neap and spring knots, and sailors turn tide tables into water depth with the rule of twelfths (1:2:3:3:2:1 of the range per hour). Tides repeat about every 12 h 25 min, so a tide table slides roughly 50 minutes a day. Tidal causeways such as Holy Island publish daily crossing windows that slide with the tide, the same timetable puzzle in real life. Minimum-time steering through a drifting current is Zermelo's problem; one 2019 arXiv paper reports analytic solutions can be unstable in turbulent flow (single source, unconfirmed), so the build searches a time-dependent grid instead. Station tables put the 2026 king-tide windows at Oct 10-11 and about Oct 26-28. The strait, ports and tide station are invented; the physics is simplified and labelled so.

facts.claim: The rule of twelfths estimates tide height between low and high water as 1/12, 2/12, 3/12, 3/12, 2/12 and 1/12 of the range in successive hours for a roughly sinusoidal semidiurnal tide, and is used to judge when a shallow bar or ledge can be crossed.

A tidal stream atlas gives one chartlet per hour relative to high water at a standard port (Dover for the southern North Sea), with arrows whose paired numbers give neap and spring rates in knots, for example 05,19 meaning 0.5 and 1.9 knots.
Holy Island's tidal causeway has dated safe-crossing windows published by Northumberland County Council, and the windows shift from day to day with the tide.
Zermelo's problem is the minimum-time steering of a vessel through a moving current, studied for boats and underwater vehicles including time-varying flows.
As of 2026-10-11, station tables list a king-tide window around the Oct 10 new moon (Oct 10-11 on US east-coast tables).
As of 2026-10-11, station tables put the larger perigean king-tide peak near the Oct 26 full moon, with the highest predicted tides mostly Oct 26-28.
Semidiurnal tides recur about every 12 h 25 min because the lunar day lasts 24 h 50 min, so high water arrives roughly 50 minutes later each day.

design.coreLoop: Each passage runs briefing, planning, sailing and review. The visitor studies the tide table, tide curve and stream atlas, picks a departure hour and up to five waypoints with an aim-off angle per leg, and sees a live prediction of the track update. Sailing plays the day at high speed while streams swing and the ledge floods or dries. Review overlays the solver ghost and arrival isochrones, scores efficiency against the optimum, and offers a harder strait or the seeded daily passage.
sophisticationHooks: Tide model with a spring-neap beat: two lunar-solar constituents plus the real moon age set height, and stream strength follows the rate of change of height, so slack water lands near high and low water.
Stream field relaxed over the hand-drawn water mask in a Worker: depth-weighted potential flow makes streams quicken through narrows and round headlands, with hand-placed eddies added.
Solver ghost: time-dependent Dijkstra on an 80 by 60 grid with waiting allowed gives the earliest arrival at every cell, which yields both the optimal route and the isochrone contours.
A drying ledge opens only when charted depth plus tide height beats the draught, so departure time, route and the rule of twelfths interlock.
design.scopeForOneDay: Eight disjoint files: tide model, stream-field solver (Worker), time-dependent route solver (Worker), boat kinematics, chart renderer, level data with a seeded daily passage, planner UI, app shell with hash state and about panel. Built: 6 invented straits, tide table and curve, atlas scrubber, ghost boat and isochrones, light and dark chart themes, reduced-motion mode. Left out: real coastlines, live tide data, wind, sound, accounts.
risks: Potential-flow streams have no true overfalls or turbulence, so copy calls them stylised and hand-placed eddies add character.
A dense planner on a 360px screen is mitigated with a bottom sheet, tap-to-add waypoints and a list-and-keyboard alternative to dragging.
Difficulty across springs and neaps needs tuning; par times come from the solver at build time rather than guesses.

Single-sourced remarks (the 2019 finding that analytic Zermelo solutions can be unstable) stay off the page; king-tide dates vary by station, so copy says 'as of 2026-10-11, per US station tables' and the page makes no forecast.
A game, not a navigation aid: all places and stations are invented and the about panel says so.

ideas.title: Breaking Changes
ideas.pitch: A plain grey brick-breaker ships as v0.1. Between waves the studio offers two release candidates written in marketing-speak, such as 'Improved ball responsiveness' or 'Ceiling deprecated to improve performance'. You decode the euphemism, pick one, and play the next wave under its real rules while a board of system lamps shows what just went offline. A codex records what each phrase actually meant, and by v1.0 your build is a loud, glorious, thoroughly broken thing you assembled yourself.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless premise, since everyone has met a vague update note, with a jam-weekend nod: one jam page reportedly lists 'Systems Offline' as its theme (as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io, unconfirmed), and each patch here switches a game system off or on.

research.summary: Hook, honestly rated: the Patch Notes jam page on itch.io lists 'Systems Offline' for a 72-hour jam on 9-12 October 2026, but the page also says theme TBA and the host's own announcements found by search only show earlier editions, so the theme is shown as reported, not confirmed, and the game stands without it. What is verified shapes the design: the 2012 juice talk by Martin Jonasson and Petri Purho showed how layers of feedback transform the feel of a plain game (its demo is reported, without a clear attribution in the results, to be a simple Breakout clone), which gives the greybox-to-gold arc and the juice ladder; two separate support forums carry user complaints about stock release-note wording, which anchors the euphemism grammar in something people recognise; a Mini Jam page reportedly rates a mandatory limitation rather than the theme, which this idea turns into a per-wave limitation delivered as a patch note. Live-service balance patches and their notes

design.coreLoop: Wave loop: you read two patch notes, pick one with 1 or 2 (or a tap), watch the system-lamp board change as its true effect applies, then play a 30 to 40 second brick-breaker wave under every rule accumulated so far. Clearing the wave or losing a ball ends the loop with a 'known issues' reveal that tells you what the euphemism really meant and files it in the codex. Notes follow a learnable grammar (improved means faster with a catch, rebalanced means nerfed, deprecated means removed with compensation, reimagined means shuffled), so minute two is decoding and minute ten is routing synergies, such as a sticky paddle with gravity, around your build's weak spots. Ten waves end in a v1.0 launch card; three rollbacks end the run early. The daily seed makes the offers identical for everyone.
sophisticationHooks: A decodable grammar: eight verbs (improved, rebalanced, streamlined, reimagined, modernized, deprecated, added in beta, fixed) act on eight game systems (ball, paddle, ceiling, bricks, gravity, input, audio, juice), so a euphemism means the same kind of change everywhere. A codex fills in as you learn, which is what separates minute two from minute ten.

Generic modifier engine with synergy and clamps: about 40 valid verb-noun pairs stack, such as a sticky paddle with gravity or multiball with the ceiling deprecated, while a stall watchdog ships an in-fiction hotfix if no brick falls for 25 seconds.

The juice ladder: feedback layers (hit-stop, squash and stretch, trails, particles, shake, synthesized sound) arrive as patches, so the page shows game feel being built from silent grey boxes at v0.1 to a bright, noisy v1.0. Each layer has a reduced-motion twin and a shake toggle.

Hero moment: a board of system lamps clicks off or on when a patch lands, an installing-update wipe sweeps the playfield, and the same bricks that were flat grey rectangles burst into confetti by v1.0 while the changelog scrolls alongside.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: fixed-step brick-breaker with sub-stepped collisions, a verb-by-noun patch engine (8 verbs, 8 systems, about 40 valid pairs) with flavor text, two-card picker, system-lamp board, codex, juice ladder with reduced-motion twins, muted-by-default WebAudio blips, ten waves with rollbacks and a v1.0 launch card, URL-hash seed and share string, keyboard and touch controls, about panel with sources. Cut first: unlockable skins, boss wave, extra brick types. Not built: leaderboards, any backend.
risks: Hook is single-sourced and inconsistent: the page shows 'Systems Offline' as reported on a jam page, as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io (unconfirmed); the game does not depend on it.
Brick-breakers are crowded: distinctness rides on the decodable verb grammar, the codex and the writing, so the spec should protect those before extra polish.
Soft-locks and balance: clamp every parameter, ship an in-fiction hotfix that reverts the last patch if no brick falls for 25 seconds, and let the QA monkey test random builds.

ideas.title: Orbital Knitwear
ideas.pitch: A visitor tunes a satellite's height, tilt and orbit shape and watches its ground track unspool across a wool-textured world map, each pass adding a ribbon of stitches wherever the camera swath reaches. Pattern cards set goals such as seeing latitudes the space station never reaches, repeating the same track every 16 days, keeping a steady local time of day, or lingering over the far north. A flat-versus-polar toggle shows how the projection decides which holes look big, while the score counts true surface area.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: orbital geometry never goes stale. The knitting frame makes a nerdy subject cozy, and the projection toggle and daylight terminator put a map argument at the centre.

research.summary: A ground track is a map argument: one orbit is a sine wave on a flat map and a spiral seen from the pole. Research shapes the mechanic. Earth's bulge (J2) turns an orbit's plane, and at about 98 degrees and 600-700 km that turn matches the Sun's 0.9856 degrees per day, so a satellite keeps one local solar time; a two-body-plus-J2 calculation done here gives 97.79 degrees at 600 km and 98.19 degrees at 700 km, matching both sources. Landsat's 16-day cycle of 233 orbits is a literal knitting gauge: tracks about 172 km apart against a 185 km swath. The ISS inclination of 51.6 degrees fences its track and Earth's spin moves each pass about 23 degrees west. Scoring by true area matters: the band poleward of 60 degrees is a third of an equirectangular map but about 13 percent of the planet (computed here). The Molniya figures are single-sourced.

facts.claim: A sun-synchronous orbit needs its node to drift about 0.9856 degrees per day to hold one local solar time; Earth's J2 bulge supplies the drift, at about 98.2 degrees inclination for a 700 km circular orbit (NASA primer) and about 97.8 degrees near 600 km (second source).

The International Space Station orbits at 51.6 degrees inclination, so it never gets farther north or south than 51.6 degrees latitude, at roughly 370-460 km altitude in orbits of 90 to 93 minutes; each pass lands about 22.9 degrees of longitude west of the last (NASA tutorial).

Landsat 4-9 fly a circular sun-synchronous orbit near 705 km on a 16-day repeat of 233 orbits; an orbit takes about 98.9 minutes, successive tracks sit about 24.7 degrees (2752 km) apart at the equator, and the design swath is 185 km.

Molniya orbits are reported to use a critical inclination of about 63.4 degrees with a 12-hour period and two apogees per day (single source, unconfirmed).

ideas.pitch: A storm has killed every screen on the boat, so the instructor turns it into a drill: you get a periscope, a stopwatch and a grease pencil. You raise the scope for a few seconds, swing it onto an unmanned target barge, turn the handwheel until the two images of its mast meet to read the range, then drop below and pencil the fix on the chart. Two fixes reveal the barge's course and speed, you slide the aim point along its track until the practice round and the barge arrive together, and a dye splash tells you how good you were.

design.coreLoop: Each drill sends one to three unmanned barges across a range at constant course and speed. You raise the scope (a spray timer limits each look), find a barge in low power, switch to high power, name its class from the recognition book and turn the handwheel until the stacked images meet to read range. You lower the scope and the fix is pencilled on the chart with bearing and clock time. You wait, look again, and the two marks give a track with an uncertainty wedge. You drag the aim point along the track until the practice round and the barge arrive together, then fire; the dye splash scores the miss distance, with bonuses for fewer looks and less exposure. Every extra look is a value-of-information bet: minute two is learning the handwheel, minute ten is choosing the gap between looks.
sophisticationHooks: Real optics: a stacked-image handwheel (two copies of the target, offset until the mast tip meets the waterline) turns a known mast height into range. The player's alignment error and a mis-identified ship class both skew the fix, and low power finds targets while high power measures.

Estimation with honesty: two timed fixes give a velocity vector drawn with an uncertainty wedge that narrows as the gap between looks grows, so waiting longer buys accuracy at the price of a barge that may sail out of range.

Equal-arrival aiming: dragging the aim point along the predicted track races two phosphor timing bars (practice round against barge) and a lamp lights when they match. A final drill takes the stadimeter away so the player must move the boat to build a baseline, as bearings-only tracking requires.

Hero moment: the scope broaches and a brass-ringed lens rises through the waterline, spray beading and clearing, horizon swaying with the swell; when the dye lands it blooms across the hull while the green readout answers with a soft afterglow. Reduced motion swaps the sway and spray for fades.

ideas.title: Eyes Only
ideas.pitch: Each plate is a mosaic of colored dots hiding a creature or a letter, and each of five simulated eyes (typical, protan, deutan, tritan, achromat) reads a different part of the picture. The visitor flips lenses, with a severity dial for milder forms, to see what each eye reveals, decodes cipher words whose letters need different eyes, and builds plates in a studio where a solver tunes the dots until exactly the chosen eyes can read them. A real lab result, dichromats out-spotting trichromats on color-camouflaged texture, inspires the masked plates, so the eye most often called deficient is the one that cracks the code.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. About 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency (as of 2026-10-11, per NEI), and the science behind the plates (camouflage-breaking studies, a 2009 simulation model) is stable and citable.

research.summary: A 1992 study reported that dichromats beat trichromats at finding texture-defined targets hidden by random red-green coloring, and a later review states dichromats do better when color is irrelevant to the task; early stimuli were stylized, so the effect is real but task-dependent. A 2009 IEEE TVCG paper by Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes gives a physiologically based simulation model covering dichromacy and anomalous trichromacy. About 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency (NEI), and deuteranomaly, a milder form, is the most common type, which motivates a severity dial. A cone-opponent view (luminance, red-green, blue-yellow) explains what each lens keeps; one paper cautions that some dichromats keep residual red-green discrimination. The design splits plates into exact ones (pure channel signals that vanish after the lens by construction) and perceptual ones (masking, labeled as a model).

design.coreLoop: A seeded plate packs about two thousand dots of mixed radii; a hidden figure is encoded as a small offset in chosen cone-contrast directions (L, M, S or luminance) with masking noise in others. The visitor switches among five lenses (keys 1 to 5) or drags a severity dial, moves a reticle to the figure, and receives a per-lens detectability readout plus a reveal card explaining which eyes could read the plate and why. Cipher mode spreads a word over plates, one letter per subset of eyes. Studio mode takes a target set of readers and runs a solver that tunes channel amplitudes and noise until the model's detectability meets the target, or reports the target infeasible. A map of all 32 reader subsets fills in as plates are made, with unreachable cells greyed out, which gives a collection goal for the tenth minute.
sophisticationHooks: Lens engine: 3x3 linear-RGB simulation matrices in the Machado style with a severity dial from typical to full dichromacy (anomalous trichromacy included), an achromat luminance lens, and self-tests (neutral gray unchanged; red-green pairs collapse under deutan and protan; blue-yellow pairs collapse under tritan).

Plate generator: seeded blue-noise circle packing with mixed radii on a spatial hash grid, figure masks from signed-distance creature shapes and a 5x7 glyph set, dot colors sampled in a cone-contrast space with gamut-safe scaling, fully deterministic from the URL hash.

Detectability model: a d-prime style score per lens (figure versus ground difference over pooled noise in the channels the lens still has) plus a clutter term where chromatic noise masks luminance signals for lenses that still see it, the Morgan-style effect; exact plates (pure channel signals) are separated from perceptual plates (masking) and labeled.

Studio solver and feasibility map: coordinate-descent search with restarts over signal mix, amplitude and per-channel noise to hit any of the 32 reader subsets; subsets that violate the channel structure are shown infeasible under the model and greyed in the map.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: lens engine and self-tests (about 250 lines), generator and renderer (about 300), detectability model and solver (about 250), UI for Hunt, Cipher and Studio modes with keyboard reticle and touch, severity dial, reveal cards, 12 specimen shapes and the glyph set, 40 curated seeds, URL-hash sharing, about and making-of panel listing verified sources only. Cut if short: sonified plate (pitch from local detectability), image import, palette tool, per-lens custom mixing.
risks: Perceptual claims: whether a typical eye misses a masked plate depends on the person and the display; the page grades by the model and labels those plates perceptual, while exact plates are true by construction.
The page is a puzzle and a model, not a vision test or diagnosis; the copy avoids telling any visitor what their own vision is.

Simulation caveats: disability-simulation critiques, residual red-green discrimination reported for some dichromats (one source, unverified), and varied displays; the about panel states them and shows the residual-discrimination point as 'as of 2026-10-11, per UC eScholarship'.

The camouflage advantage is documented for stylized stimuli and specific tasks (per a review in the search results), so the copy states it as a lab result and makes no general claim about colorblind people.
Matrix constants have to be reproduced from the published model without opening it; the fallback derives lenses from an LMS projection and the self-tests check neutrals and confusion-pair collapse.
A visual puzzle is not fully playable by blind visitors; text reveal cards and the optional sonified plate (cut if short) are the mitigation.

ideas.title: Pick Autopsy
ideas.pitch: A visitor drafts a deck of about ten cards for a tiny invented deckbuilder, choosing, skipping or trimming at four forks, and a worker then plays that deck ten thousand seeded runs, painting a 100-by-100 field of wins and losses in a blink. The autopsy replays every fork both ways and splits the win-rate change fairly across the four choices, so the visitor sees which pick carried the run, which was a decoy and which quietly cost points, each with an honest error bar. Ranking the forks before the reveal earns an intuition grade, and any pixel replays its run card by card.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. Deckbuilder folklore (skip rewards, thin the deck, trust the combo) tends to be argued from the runs a player happens to remember, and this page measures it for one invented game with ten thousand runs per fork. Genre backdrop, reported and unconfirmed: Slay the Spire 2 has been in Early Access since 2026-03-05 per the studio's news post.

research.summary: Fan guides for Slay the Spire treat skipping card rewards and trimming starter Strikes and Defends as a deliberate way to keep a deck thin (one guide suggests staying under about 15 cards unless the deck leans on card draw); guides and forums reportedly disagree on the right size, per a blended search summary, so that point is shown as reported. Opening-hand and draw odds follow the hypergeometric distribution (several trading-card math pages). Deck testers say comparing win rates by hand needs far more games than people play. Methods: the Shapley value averages a choice's marginal contribution over all orderings and the parts sum exactly to the total, which for four forks needs only 16 deck variants; common random numbers are the textbook way to compare simulations. Derived by the scout in a throwaway seeded Node prototype of an invented game, not from the web: 10,000 runs took about 0.13 s, a 16-variant batch 2 to 3.5 s, Shapley parts summed to the total in 8 of 8 scenarios, and matched seeds cut variance only 2 to 24 percent for single-card swaps, so accuracy rests on run count.

ideas.title: Shuffle Sharp
ideas.pitch: A lazy dealer riffles a fresh 52-card deck once or twice and a visitor, playing the sharp, calls each next card as it turns over. After a single idealised riffle about 31 cards can be called against 4.5 for blind guessing (the scout's seeded count), and each extra shuffle melts that edge until it is near half a card at seven riffles. A feint mode adds false shuffles and perfect faros that only look mixed, and an exact curve shows why seven is the magic number.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. A famous result becomes something felt in the fingers: exploiting a lazy shuffle is the card-table version of exploiting a strategy that mixes too little, and the curve is the plain-language picture of unexploitable play. In board-game deckbuilders every reshuffle of a hand-shuffled discard pile is a place where order can leak.

research.summary: After k riffles a deck holds only arrangements with at most 2^k rising sequences, and the chance of an arrangement depends only on its rising-sequence count r as C(2^k + n - r, n) over 2^(kn); the scout checked this law by exhaustive enumeration for small decks. Exact 52-card total variation distance (computed by the scout from Eulerian numbers) is 1.000 through k=4, then 0.924, 0.614, 0.334, 0.167, 0.085, 0.043 for k=5 to 10, matching the often-cited rule of about seven riffles (Harvey Mudd, MathWorks, Science News, the Bayer-Diaconis paper). Card guessing with complete feedback after one riffle is studied in several papers; the scout's seeded count for 52 cards gives 31.1 correct for a heads-tracking guesser (an exact Bayes guesser for one riffle matches at 31.2) against 4.5 for blind guessing, then 19.6, 12.9, 8.8, 6.6, 5.5, 5.0, 4.8, 4.7, 4.6 for 2 to 10 riffles. Eight perfect out-faros restore 52 cards (several sources; scout recount agrees).

design.coreLoop: A lazy dealer riffles a fresh deck k times (k hidden at first) and the visitor calls each next card from a tray of the unseen cards in original order, with every reveal acting as feedback. After the round the page shows hits against blind chance and a heads-tracking bot on the same shuffle, plus an exact likelihood table over k from the deck's rising-sequence count. A feint mode adds false shuffles and perfect faros to be called out, and a sweep plots the edge against the number of riffles beside the exact distance-from-random curve so the point where the edge dies is visible.
sophisticationHooks: Exact math in the page: the riffle law by rising-sequence count, 52-card total variation distance via Eulerian numbers in BigInt, and a posterior over the number of riffles after each round, all checked against enumeration for small decks
Seeded Monte Carlo edge curve (hits versus 1 to 10 riffles) in a worker with stated sample size and standard errors, drawn beside the exact distance curve
Bot honesty: an exact Bayes guesser for one riffle and a labelled heads-tracking heuristic for more, never described as optimal beyond one riffle
Feint mode: false shuffle and perfect faro (order 8 for 52 cards) versus real riffles, judged by the rising-sequence statistic; challenge links carry the seed in the URL hash
design.scopeForOneDay: In one morning the team builds: the riffle sampler and exact formulas with node self-checks (small-deck enumeration, the TV table, faro orders, known guess averages); the card tray and reveal UI with keyboard and touch; a canvas riffle animation; a worker for the edge curve; the round report with likelihood table; feint mode; an about panel with dated sources; hash state for seed and settings; light and dark; reduced motion. Cut: sound, overhand and pile shuffles, multiplayer, any deckbuilder clump panel if time is short, decks other than 52 and a 24-card phone mini deck.
risks: The seven-shuffles figure depends on the distance measure; a search summary mentioned another analysis with an information-based minimum near six shuffles, which is unconfirmed and not shown as fact. The page names total variation as its measure and plots the whole curve instead of declaring one magic number.

The riffle model is idealised; the claim that it fits real human shuffling is reported in the literature but rests on one unattributed search summary, so the page labels the model as idealised and shows that claim only as reported.
Calling cards among 52 on a 360px screen needs a compact tray design (rainbow-ordered tiles with unseen cards lit); a 24-card phone mini deck is the fallback.

Beyond one riffle the guesser is a heuristic, not a solver: its averages are computed by the page and labelled as such, and the literature suggests the best strategy is not settled in general (single result).
Framing: math and stage-magic lore only, with no money, chips, real casino or brand names; the false-shuffle content stays at the level of general knowledge about why order survives a shuffle.
Unverified items stay flagged: the Dominion-style reshuffle rule rests on one wiki result and appears as context only.
